NO-POACH / NO-HIRE AGREEMENT BETWEEN BUSINESSES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

RESTRICTION
This is a restraint between two businesses -- Acme, Inc. and Beta Staffing, Inc. -- rather than a promise by an individual worker. During the term of the parties' business relationship and for 12 months after it ends, neither Acme, Inc. nor Beta Staffing, Inc. will solicit, recruit, or hire any person who is, or was during the preceding twelve months, an employee or independent contractor of the other party, without that party's prior written consent. This is a separate question from a departing individual employee's own promise not to recruit former co-workers, which is addressed in a different document in this set.

CALIFORNIA'S GENERAL RULE AGAINST RESTRAINTS OF TRADE
California law voids, as a restraint of trade, contracts that restrain anyone from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business -- a rule not limited to noncompete clauses in individual employment contracts. On its face, the statute reaches "every contract" fitting that description, of any kind, unless a specific statutory exception applies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(a) (Leginfo official text), California Business and Professions Code section 16600, subdivision (a) (as amended by Stats. 2023, ch. 828, § 1 (AB 1076), eff. Jan. 1, 2024) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=16600.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: The statute's own text does not confine this general voidness rule to the employment relationship; a separate subdivision (quoted in the next clause) confirms that reach. A different part of this same statutory chapter carries narrow exceptions not addressed here (for example, restraints tied to the sale of a business's goodwill or the dissolution of a partnership or LLC) -- this document does not evaluate whether any such exception could apply to a particular no-hire arrangement. This is California law only; other states treat business-to-business no-hire and no-poach agreements differently, including some that permit them if reasonable in scope.

THIS RULE IS NOT LIMITED TO CONTRACTS THE RESTRAINED WORKER SIGNED
This restraint-of-trade rule is not limited to contracts to which the restrained person is a party. A contract between two businesses -- neither of which is the worker whose hiring or job mobility the contract restricts -- can still fall within this rule; the statute says so directly, in a subdivision added specifically to address that scenario.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section shall not be limited to contracts where the person being restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business is a party to the contract."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(c) (Leginfo official text), California Business and Professions Code section 16600, subdivision (c) (as amended by Stats. 2023, ch. 828, § 1 (AB 1076), eff. Jan. 1, 2024) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=16600.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: This subdivision was added to the statute effective January 1, 2024 (by AB 1076); it states that it 'does not constitute a change in, but is declaratory of, existing law' as to the broad-reading directive in the surrounding subdivision, but the third-party-reach language itself is a more recent textual addition. Separately, federal antitrust law offers an independent framework that can also apply to a business-to-business no-hire agreement, evaluated under different tests than this state statute -- litigation between two competing healthcare staffing companies over a non-solicitation-of-employees provision in their business collaboration agreement has been reported as applying federal Sherman Act rule-of-reason analysis (treating such a provision as not automatically unlawful, unlike this statute's near-automatic voidness rule) rather than California Business and Professions Code section 16600. This document does not cite a specific opinion for that antitrust analysis: this research session located secondary reporting describing that Ninth Circuit litigation but could not locate and independently verify a quotable opinion text for it through the primary-source channels available, so no case citation is given for it. Where both frameworks could apply to the same agreement, they are separate bodies of law with separate tests and can reach different results.

STATE ENFORCEMENT INTEREST IN BUSINESS-TO-BUSINESS NO-POACH PROVISIONS
Business-to-business no-hire and no-poach provisions -- including those between a franchisor and its franchisees, or among a franchisor's franchisees -- have also drawn attention from state enforcement authorities as a competition and worker-mobility concern, separate from private contract litigation between the businesses themselves. In March 2019, California's Attorney General announced settlements with several national franchise companies requiring them to stop including no-poach provisions of this kind in their franchise agreements.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Many of these anticompetitive no-poach provisions required franchise operators to contractually agree to not hire or solicit the employees of another franchise operator."
  — California Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General, press release, Attorney General Becerra Announces Multistate Settlements Targeting "No-Poach" Policies that Harm Workers (Cal. DOJ, published Mar. 12, 2019) (https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/attorney-general-becerra-announces-multistate-settlements-targeting-%E2%80%9Cno-poach%E2%80%9D)
  Known gap: This reflects a settlement of enforcement claims, not a court ruling interpreting Business and Professions Code section 16600 or any other statute -- it establishes no binding legal test, and its terms bind only the companies that signed it. Other states' attorneys general participated in the same multistate settlement, and separate, later settlements covering other franchise companies were announced afterward; this document cites only the March 2019 announcement covering four named companies as one verifiable example, not a complete account of all such state enforcement activity.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate agreement to these terms.

Acme, Inc.
By: _______________________
Date: September 1, 2026

Beta Staffing, Inc.
By: _______________________
Date: _______________

Executed in Oakland, California.

—
